title: MySQL Compared with SQLite and PostgreSQL
summary: Compare MySQL with SQLite and PostgreSQL: architecture, types, auto-increment ids, upserts, RETURNING, string handling, case sensitivity, JSON and concurrency, with the same tasks written three ways.
introduction: Most developers meet more than one database: SQLite in tests and mobile apps, PostgreSQL on one project, MySQL on the next. The core SQL is shared, but each has a personality, and the differences hide in exactly the places where copied code fails silently. This closing lesson puts MySQL 8.4 and 9 side by side with SQLite 3 and current PostgreSQL, with the same tasks written three ways, so you know what to translate and when each database is the right choice.
learningObjectives: Contrast the server model of MySQL and PostgreSQL with the embedded model of SQLite
Translate auto-increment ids, upserts, RETURNING and string concatenation between the three
Predict how case sensitivity, booleans and dates differ
Choose the right database for a project

rows: A library inside your program; the database is one file
One writer at a time, many readers
Fixed column types, strict mode by default
Flexible unless the table is declared `STRICT`

blocks.text: The architecture decides the first question: SQLite is for data that belongs to one program on one machine; MySQL and PostgreSQL are for data shared by many clients over a network, with accounts, backups and replication to match.

Auto-numbered keys, enumerations and money are where table definitions diverge most. `AUTO_INCREMENT` is MySQL's spelling; PostgreSQL uses identity columns; in SQLite an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` is an alias for the row id and numbers itself.

blocks.text: SQLite prints nothing on success. It has no decimal type, so money is best kept as integer cents, and `STRICT` (SQLite 3.37 and later) makes it reject a string in an integer column, which plain SQLite would happily store.
Inserting and reading back the id

PostgreSQL and SQLite return generated values from the `INSERT` itself with `RETURNING`. MySQL has no such clause: run the insert, then ask for `LAST_INSERT_ID()`, which is safe because it is tracked per connection. The customer below becomes id 7 in the roastery data, because id 6 was used and deleted in the [CRUD lesson](/tutorials/mysql/crud).

PostgreSQL and SQLite

blocks.text: MySQL's `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` reacts to *any* unique key that conflicts; the standard-style `ON CONFLICT` used by PostgreSQL and SQLite names the columns and reads the attempted values as `excluded`. Both update Noor's city here; MySQL reports 2 affected rows for an update through this path.

blocks.title: MySQL
PostgreSQL and SQLite

blocks.text: String concatenation is the classic porting bug: `||` concatenates in PostgreSQL and SQLite but means OR in MySQL, as the [introduction](/tutorials/mysql/introduction) showed. Use `CONCAT`, which the other two also support, or turn on `PIPES_AS_CONCAT` for the session when you must run shared SQL.

Case is the subtler difference. MySQL's default collation compares text case-insensitively, so two spellings are equal unless you ask for a binary collation; PostgreSQL compares exactly and offers `ILIKE` for case-insensitive patterns; SQLite's `=` is exact while its `LIKE` ignores case for ASCII letters only.

blocks.code:
SELECT 'Mei' = 'mei' AS same_letters,
       'Mei' COLLATE utf8mb4_bin = 'mei' AS same_bytes;

blocks.text: Identifier quoting differs too: MySQL uses backticks, the other two use double quotes. MySQL accepts double quotes for identifiers only when `sql_mode` includes `ANSI_QUOTES`; otherwise `"name"` is a string.

blocks.title: Testing on SQLite, deploying on MySQL
blocks.text: Running the test suite against SQLite because it needs no server hides MySQL-specific bugs: a `UNIQUE` index that SQLite treats case-sensitively and MySQL does not, a `VARCHAR(50)` that SQLite never enforces, a `GROUP BY` that MySQL rejects under `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY`, a `||` that MySQL reads as OR. Run at least the integration tests against the same MySQL version as production, for example in the Docker container from the [installation lesson](/tutorials/mysql/installing-connecting).

rows: `LIMIT n OFFSET m` or `LIMIT m, n`

items: **SQLite** when the data lives with one program: desktop and mobile apps, command-line tools, embedded devices, local caches and test fixtures. Zero administration, but one writer at a time.

**PostgreSQL** when you want the richest SQL: window functions and CTEs are shared with MySQL, but PostgreSQL adds arrays, range types, transactional DDL, extensions such as PostGIS, and the strictest standards compliance. Our [PostgreSQL tutorial](/tutorials/postgresql) starts there.

**MySQL** when you want the largest ecosystem of hosting, tooling and hiring, straightforward replication, and the engine behind WordPress, Drupal, Magento and most PHP and Rails hosting. MariaDB, a community fork, shares the client protocol but has diverged in features and syntax, so check the [MariaDB tutorial](/tutorials/mariadb) before assuming parity.

blocks.title: Where to go next
blocks.text: Practise standard SQL in the browser with the [SQL tutorial](/tutorials/sql), then compare the [SQLite](/tutorials/sqlite) and [PostgreSQL](/tutorials/postgresql) tutorials. The [MySQL reference](/references/mysql) and [examples](/examples/mysql) collect the syntax from these lessons for daily use.

questions.question: Which database runs inside your program as a library rather than as a server?
questions.explanation: SQLite is an embedded library that reads and writes a single file. MySQL and PostgreSQL are server processes that clients connect to over a network.

questions.question: To make `||` concatenate strings in a MySQL session, add `___` to `sql_mode`.
questions.explanation: PIPES_AS_CONCAT changes || from logical OR to string concatenation. CONCAT() works regardless and is the portable choice.
